Zeus swallowed his own wife. She was pregnant.
He did it on purpose. And an ancient Greek poem tells us why.
This was after Zeus had won a ten-year war. After he had thrown down a monster with a hundred heads. After the other gods had urged him to be their king.
To see why, we have to go back to the first ruler of the sky. And to a warning he gave his own sons.
On the way, we will find a stone that was fed to a god. And a painter who drew the monster very differently from the poet.
The poem is the Theogony, by a Greek poet named Hesiod. Most scholars date it to about seven hundred B.C.
The story of the world begins with Chaos. Then Gaia, the Earth. And from Gaia comes Ouranos, the Sky, made just as big as she is, so that he can cover her on every side.
Gaia and Ouranos have children. Twelve of them are Titans. Three are Cyclopes, one-eyed makers of the thunderbolt. And three are Hundred-Handers, giants with a hundred arms and fifty heads each.
Ouranos hates the three Hundred-Handers most of all. And he hides his children away inside Gaia, as each one is born.
Gaia groans, cramped with her own children. So she makes a sickle out of grey flint, and asks her sons to use it on their father.
They are all too scared to answer. All but one. Cronos, the youngest, the clever one.
Gaia hides Cronos in ambush, and puts the sickle in his hand. When Ouranos comes at night, Cronos strikes. And Cronos takes his father's place.

Ouranos has one thing left to say. He calls his sons Titans, as an insult. Hesiod says the word comes from a verb meaning to strain, because, Ouranos says, they strained too far, and did a terrible thing.
And he promises that one day, someone will pay for it.
Cronos is king now. And he has learned a prophecy from Gaia and Ouranos. One day, his own son will overcome him.
So Cronos makes a rule. Every child that his wife Rhea bears, he swallows as it is born.
Five children. Hestia. Demeter. Hera. Hades. Poseidon.
Rhea's grief never ends. When she is about to bear a sixth, she goes to her own parents, Gaia and Ouranos, and asks for a plan.
They send her to Crete. In a cave on a mountain, Gaia takes the baby from her, and hides him.
To Cronos, Gaia gives a great stone, wrapped in baby clothes. He takes it. He swallows it. And he never notices.
That baby is Zeus. The youngest. The one who was not eaten.
Hesiod skips ahead. The boy grows strong. Gaia tricks Cronos, and Zeus overpowers him. That is all the poem says about how the gods got free.
Cronos throws them all back up. The stone comes first, because it was swallowed last.
Zeus plants that stone in the ground at Pytho, another name for Delphi, below Mount Parnassus, so that people will see it and wonder.
More than eight hundred years later, a Greek traveller named Pausanias visits Delphi. And he finds a small stone.
Every day, he writes, the locals pour olive oil over it. At every feast, they lay raw wool on it. And some say this is the stone that was given to Cronos in place of his child.
Zeus also frees his uncles, the Cyclopes, who have been chained up. They thank him with thunder, lightning, and the thunderbolt. Until then, Gaia had hidden the thunder away.
Now the war. The Titans hold Mount Othrys. Zeus and the young gods hold Olympus.
Hesiod does not say what started it. He only says they fight for ten full years, and neither side can win.
Then Gaia speaks again. She tells the gods that with the three Hundred-Handers on their side, they will win. But the Hundred-Handers are still chained under the earth, where Ouranos put them.
So Zeus and the gods bring them up to the light. Then they give them everything they need. Nectar and ambrosia, the food of the gods.
Their spirit comes back. Zeus reminds them how he freed them, and asks them to show their strength. Cottus, one of the three, answers for all of them. They will fight.
The sea rings. The earth crashes. Olympus shakes on its foundations, and the shock reaches all the way down to Tartarus, the pit beneath the world.
And now Zeus stops holding back. He comes down from Olympus, hurling lightning. The forests crackle. The sea starts to boil. The heat, Hesiod says, seizes Chaos itself.
The Hundred-Handers throw three hundred rocks, one on top of another. They bury the Titans beneath the earth, and bind them.
Ouranos had promised that someone would pay. Now the Titans are paying.
How deep is Tartarus? Hesiod gives a measurement. A bronze anvil dropped from the sky takes nine days to reach the earth, and nine more to reach Tartarus.
Poseidon fits gates of bronze to the prison. And in one passage, Hesiod has the three Hundred-Handers stay on as its guards.

In Hesiod's telling, the freed prisoners are the key to the victory. For ten years, the young gods could not win alone. Ouranos had chained these three. Zeus and the gods freed them, fed them, and asked for their help.
The Titans are locked away. But the poem is not finished.
Gaia bears one more child, her youngest. Typhoeus. His father is Tartarus, the pit itself.
Hesiod gives him a hundred snake heads, with dark, flickering tongues, and fire flashing from the eyes of every one.
And a voice in every head. Sometimes it makes a sound the gods can understand. Sometimes it bellows like a bull, or roars like a lion, or yelps like puppies, or hisses until the mountains ring.
That day, Hesiod says, something past help would have happened. Typhoeus would have ruled over gods and mortals, if Zeus had not noticed him in time.
Zeus thunders. Olympus shakes. Hades trembles in the underworld, and the Titans tremble in Tartarus. Then Zeus leaps down from Olympus and burns every one of those heads.
Typhoeus crashes down, burned and broken, and the earth groans. The ground itself melts, Hesiod says, like tin. And Zeus throws him into Tartarus.
From Typhoeus come the storm winds, the ones that scatter ships and wreck sailors. Only three winds are not his: the north wind, the south wind, and the west wind.
It is a water jar, a hydria, painted around five hundred and forty B.C. That is roughly a century and a half after Hesiod, by the usual dates. It sits in a museum in Munich.
On the left, Zeus, with a thunderbolt raised in his hand. His name is painted beside him.
On the right, the monster. The painter gave him a human face, huge wings, and a body of coiling snakes.
Hesiod gave him a hundred snake heads, and never mentions wings.
Maybe a painter simply has the curve of a pot to work with.
Now the war is over, and the monster is gone.
After the war, the gods urge Zeus to rule over them. And Gaia is the one who prompts them.
Cronos took his father's place with a sickle in his hand. Zeus is urged.
He divides the honors among the gods. Each one gets a share. And then he marries.
His first wife is Metis. Hesiod says she is wiser than all gods and all mortals.
Metis is about to give birth to Athena. That is when Zeus deceives her with cunning words, and puts her inside his own belly.
He does it on the advice of Gaia and Ouranos. And the reason is stated plainly: so that no one else will ever take Zeus's place as king.
Because Metis is destined to have two children. First, a daughter, as strong as her father, and as wise. And after her, a son with an overbearing spirit, who would be king of gods and men.
Zeus does not wait for the son to grow up. He does not wait for the son to be born. He swallows the mother.
Ouranos chained some of his children. Cronos swallowed his. Zeus swallowed the mother, before the son could exist.

And notice who gives the advice. Gaia made the sickle. Gaia hid the baby. Gaia tricked Cronos. Gaia told the gods how to win the war. Gaia prompted them to make Zeus king. And Gaia, with Ouranos, tells Zeus how to make sure that nobody ever takes his place.
Again and again in this poem, Gaia is behind the turns of power.
Three rulers of the sky. The first was struck down by his son. The second was overthrown by his. The third made sure that the child who could do it to him was never born.
Hesiod passes no judgment. He calls it a deception, done with cunning words, and moves on. And right after, Zeus marries again.
But the poem leaves a puzzle. Metis was swallowed before Athena was born. And yet, a little further on, Hesiod says that Zeus himself gave birth to Athena, from his own head.
